'''''Hesperocyparis macrocarpa''''' also known as '''''Cupressus macrocarpa''''',<ref>{{Cite web|last=Bartel|first=Jim A.|date=2012|title=Hesperocyparis macrocarpa|url=https://ucjeps.berkeley.edu/eflora/eflora_display.php?tid=89298|url-status=live|access-date=4 October 2021|website=Jepson eFlora|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170828195801/http://ucjeps.berkeley.edu/eflora/eflora_display.php?tid=89298 |archive-date=2017-08-28 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |author1=Robert P. Adams |author2=Jim A. Bartel |author3=Robert A. Price |year=2009 |title=A new genus, ''Hesperocyparis'', for the cypresses of the Western Hemisphere |journal=[[Phytologia]] |volume=91 |issue=1 |pages=160–185 |url=http://www.phytologia.org/uploads/2/3/4/2/23422706/911160-185adamsbartelhesperocyparis.pdf }}</ref> or the '''Monterey cypress''' is a species of [[Conifer|coniferous]] tree in the cypress family, [[Cupressaceae]]. It is endemic to [[California]].

The Monterey cypress is found naturally only on the [[Central Coast (California)|Central Coast of California]]. Due to being a [[glacial relict]], the natural distributional range of the species during modern times is confined to two small relict populations near [[Carmel-by-the-Sea, California|Carmel]], [[California]], at Cypress Point in [[Pebble Beach, California|Pebble Beach]] and at [[Point Lobos]].<ref>C. Michael Hogan & Michael P. Frankis. 2009. [http://www.globaltwitcher.com/artspec_information.asp?thingid=62524 ''Monterey Cypress: Cupressus macrocarpa'', GlobalTwitcher.com ed. N. Stromberg] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170906035305/http://www.globaltwitcher.com/artspec_information.asp?thingid=62524 |date=2017-09-06 }}</ref>  Historically during the peak of the last ice age, Monterey cypress would have likely comprised a much larger forest that extended much further north and south.<ref name=":0">Axelrod, D. I. (1982). [http://www.jstor.org/stable/41424365 Age and origin of the Monterey endemic area.] ''Madroño'', ''29''(3), 127–147.</ref>

== Description ==
[[File:Monterey Cypress in Carmel, Calif., 1916.jpeg|thumb|Monterey Cypress near Carmel, Calif., 1916]]
''Hesperocyparis macrocarpa'' is a medium-sized [[conifer]]ous [[evergreen]] [[tree]], which often becomes irregular and flat-topped as a result of the strong winds that are typical of its [[native species|native]] area. It grows to heights of up to 40 meters (133 feet) in perfect growing conditions, and its trunk diameter can reach 2.5 meters (over 8 feet). The foliage grows in dense sprays which are bright green in color and release a deep lemony aroma when crushed. The [[leaf|leaves]] are scale-like, 2–5 mm long, and produced on rounded (not flattened) shoots; seedlings up to a year old have needle-like leaves 4–8 mm long.

The seed [[conifer cone|cones]] are globose to oblong, 20–40 mm long, with 6–14 scales, green at first, maturing brown about 20–24 months after pollination. The pollen cones are 3–5 mm long, and release their [[pollen]] in late winter or early spring.<ref name=farjon /><ref name=fna /><ref name=rushforthc>{{cite book |author=K. Rushforth |year=1987 |title=Conifers |publisher=Helm |isbn=0-7470-2801-X}}</ref> The [[binomial nomenclature|specific epithet]] ''macrocarpa'' (from [[Greek language|Greek]]) means "with large fruit".<ref name=RHSLG>{{cite book |last=Harrison |first=Lorraine |title=RHS Latin for Gardeners |year=2012 |publisher=Mitchell Beazley |location=United Kingdom |isbn=978-1845337315 }}</ref>

Because of the large trunk size some trees develop, people have assumed that individual ''H. macrocarpa'' trees may be up to 2,000 years old.  However, the longest-lived report based on physical evidence is only 284 years old.<ref>{{cite book |author=Willis Linn Jepson |year=1923 |title=The Trees of California |edition=2nd |publisher=[[University of California Press]] |page=75 |url=http://www.cupressus.net/Jepson1923a.html|author-link=Willis Linn Jepson }}</ref> The renowned Californian botanist [[Willis Linn Jepson]] wrote that "the advertisement of [''C. macrocarpa'' trees] in seaside literature as 1,000 to 2,000 years old does not ... rest upon any actual data, and probably represents a desire to minister to a popular craving for superlatives".<ref>{{cite book |editor=Joseph H. Engbeck |year=1919|title=Point Lobos Reserve State Park, California: Interpretation of a Primitive Landscape |publisher=University of California |author=Willis Linn Jepson |chapter=Appendix I: scientific notes on the Monterey cypress |pages=86–87 |chapter-url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/29199#page/93/mode/1up|author-link=Willis Linn Jepson}}</ref>  Few trees survive beyond 100 years. As a counterpoint to this, many of the earliest introductions of the species into New Zealand around 1860 still survive and the major cause of mortality of these cultivated specimens is felling.<ref>{{cite book |author=S.W. Burstall & E.V. Sale |year=1984 |title=Great Trees of New Zealand |publisher=A.H. & A.W. Reed Ltd| page = 95 |isbn=0-589-01532-X }}</ref> One such example is the 160 year old St. Barnabas Church tree in Stoke, Nelson, New Zealand.<ref>{{cite web | url = http://register.notabletrees.org.nz/tree/view/1342 | work = The Zealand Tree Register | title = Tree Information | access-date = 30 January 2020}}</ref>

== Taxonomy ==
''Hesperocyparis macrocarpa'' was given its first scientific description by the German botanist [[Karl Theodor Hartweg]] with the name ''Cupressus macrocarpa''.<ref name="POWO" /> Hartweg's trip to California coincided with the [[Mexican–American War]]. He observed in his report, "Under these circumstances I cannot venture far away from Monterey, nor is it advisable that I should do so, as I might fall in with a party of country people, who could not be persuaded that a person would come all the way from London to look after weeds, which in their opinion are not worth picking up, but might suppose that I have some political object in view; I, therefore, confine my excursions within a few miles of the town." In July 1846 he observed the Monterey cypress trees and named them, though his paper was not received in London until 10 May of the following year.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hartweg |first1=Karl Theodor |title=Journal of a Mission to California in Search of Plants Part. III |journal=The Journal of the Horticultural Society of London |date=1847 |volume=2 |page=187 |url=https://archive.org/details/journalofhorticu02hort_0/page/187 |access-date=11 February 2024 |location=London |language=en}}</ref>

Along with other New World ''Cupressus'' species, it has recently been transferred to the genus ''[[Hesperocyparis]]'', on genetic evidence that the New World ''Cupressus'' (NWC) are not very closely related to the Old World ''Cupressus'' (OWC) species.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Damon P. Little|year=2006|title=Evolution and circumscription of the true cypresses (Cupressaceae: ''Cupressus'')|journal=[[Systematic Botany]]|volume=31|issue=3|pages=461–480|doi=10.1600/036364406778388638|jstor=25064176}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|author1=Robert P. Adams|author2=Jim A. Bartel|author3=Robert A. Price|year=2009|title=A new genus, ''Hesperocyparis'', for the cypresses of the Western Hemisphere|url=http://www.phytologia.org/uploads/2/3/4/2/23422706/911160-185adamsbartelhesperocyparis.pdf|journal=[[Phytologia]]|volume=91|issue=1|pages=160–185}}</ref>

''Hesperocyparis macrocarpa'' is a [[Paleoendemism|paleoendemic]], with fossilized remains discovered in [[Drakes Bay]] and [[Rancho La Brea]] evidencing a much larger extent in the past.<ref name=":0" />

Phylogenetic analysis of nuclear DNA sequences and organismic data recover distinct lineages, with the NWC being sister to [[Juniper|''Juniperus'']] or ''Juniperus'' and the OWC.<ref>Terry, R. G., & Adams, R. P. (2015). A molecular re-examination of phylogenetic relationships among Juniperus, Cupressus, and the Hesperocyparis-Callitropsis-Xanthocyparis clades of Cupressaceae. ''Phytologia'', ''97''(1), 66-74.</ref> However, chloroplast sequences sometimes place both OWC and NWC with a [[common descent|common ancestor]], possibly due to ancient [[Hybrid (biology)|hybridization]].<ref>Yang, Z. Y., Ran, J. H., & Wang, X. Q. (2012). [https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1055790312001704 Three genome-based phylogeny of Cupressaceae sl: further evidence for the evolution of gymnosperms and Southern Hemisphere biogeography]. ''Molecular Phylogenetics and Evolution'', ''64''(3), 452-470.</ref> Other more obvious [[Morphology (biology)|morphological]] differences support their separation, such as the presence of 3 to 5 [[cotyledon]]s in NWC, as opposed to 2 in Old World species, [[glaucous]] seed coats, and [[Polymorphism (biology)|monomorphic]] leaves on ultimate branch segments.<ref name=":1">Terry, R. G., Pyne, M. I., Bartel, J. A., & Adams, R. P. (2016). [https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Randall-Terry/publication/301832103_A_molecular_biogeography_of_the_New_World_cypresses_Callitropsis_Hesperocyparis_Cupressaceae/links/572c9f5b08ae9e18450dbd2b/A-molecular-biogeography-of-the-New-World-cypresses-Callitropsis-Hesperocyparis-Cupressaceae.pdf A molecular biogeography of the New World cypresses (Callitropsis, Hesperocyparis; Cupressaceae)]. ''Plant Systematics and Evolution'', ''302''(7), 921-942.</ref>

Analysis of phylogenetic relationships show that the species is placed within the ''Macrocarpa'' clade, which diverged from the ''Arizonica'' clade, both within ''Hesperocyparis''. The two clades are separated biogeographically by the [[Transverse Ranges]], which forms a barrier to any north–south migration of most species within these clades.<ref name=":1" />

== Distribution ==
[[File:Artsey cypress.jpg|thumb|Trees showing the species' typical wind-sculpted habit in its native area]]
[[File:2016-06-03 USA, CA, Carmel Beach DSC 8536 DxO.jpg|thumb|Monterey cypress trees in fog near Carmel Beach, CA, USA]]
The two native [[cypress forest]] stands are protected, within [[Point Lobos|Point Lobos State Natural Reserve]] and [[Del Monte Forest, California|Del Monte Forest]]. The natural habitat is noted for its cool, moist summers, frequently enveloping the trees in [[sea]] [[fog]].<ref name=farjon>Farjon, A. (2005). ''Monograph of Cupressaceae and Sciadopitys''. Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew. {{ISBN|1-84246-068-4}}</ref><ref name=fna>{{eFloras|1|233500460|Cupressus macrocarpa |first=James E. |last=Eckenwalder |volume=2}}</ref>

This species has been widely planted outside its native range, particularly along the coasts of California and Oregon.  Its [[Europe]]an distribution includes [[Great Britain]] (including the [[Isle of Man]] and the [[Channel Islands]]), [[France]], [[Ireland]], [[Greece]], [[Italy]] and [[Portugal]].<ref>{{Flora Europaea |genus=Cupressus |species=macrocarpa}}</ref> In [[New Zealand]], plantings have [[naturalisation (biology)|naturalized]], finding conditions there more favorable than in its native range. It has also been grown experimentally as a timber crop in [[Kenya]].<ref name=farjon /><ref name=rushforthc />

The tree has been successfully planted in [[Sri Lanka]], with a 130-year old specimen on view at the [[Hakgala Botanical Garden]] in [[Nuwara Eliya]].<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.palmtalk.org/forum/topic/37404-monterey-cypress-in-sri-lanka/ | title=Monterey cypress in Sri Lanka | date=18 June 2013 }}</ref>

''Hesperocyparis macrocarpa'' is also grown in [[South Africa]].<ref>{{Cite book|last=Sim|first=Thomas Robertson|title=Tree Planting in Natal|publisher=Pietermaritzburg : P. Davis|year=1905|series=Natal. Dept. of Agriculture. Bulletin, 7}}</ref> For example, a [[coppicing|copse]] has been planted to commemorate South African infantrymen who died in the Allied cause in Italy and [[North Africa]] during World War 2. As in California, the Cape trees are gnarled and wind-sculpted.

Monterey Cypress has been introduced to the [[Falkland Islands]], where it exists in a small forest at [[Hill Cove]] and another at [[Carcass Island]].

== Cultivation and uses ==
[[File:Chiparos de Monterey-Cupressus macrocarpa.jpg|thumb|upright|The tallest Monterey cypress on the [[Isle of Wight]], planted in the early 1850s.]]
Monterey cypress has been widely cultivated away from its native range, both elsewhere along the California coast, and in other areas with similar cool summer, mild winter oceanic climates. It was very early cultivated in the United Kingdom. In 1846 Karl Hartweg sent the [[Royal Horticultural Society]] seeds along with a report on his journeys in California.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Dunn |first1=Malcolm |title=The Value in the British Islands of Introduced Conifers |journal=Journal of the Royal Horticultural Society |date=1892 |volume=14 |page=90 |url=https://archive.org/details/journalofroyalho14roya/page/90 |access-date=12 February 2024 |publisher=Royal Horticultural Society |location=London}}</ref> It is a popular private garden and public landscape tree in California. It is so widely planted in [[Golden Gate Park]] that the silhouette of the tree is sometimes printed as a symbol of the park.<ref>{{cite web|title=Lands End Poster|url=https://store.parksconservancy.org/collections/lands-end|publisher=Golden Gate National Parks Conservancy|accessdate=2 April 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite web archived|title=Golden Gate Park|url=https://goldengatepark.com/|publisher=GoldenGatePark.com|accessdate=2 April 2021|archive-date=21 January 2016|url-status=dead}}</ref>

When planted in areas with hot summers, for example in interior California away from the coastal fog belt, Monterey cypress has proved highly susceptible to [[cypress canker]], caused by the [[fungus]] ''Seiridium cardinale'', and rarely survives more than a few years. This disease is not a problem where summers are cool.<ref>{{cite journal |author=W. W. Wagener |year=1948 |title=Diseases of Cypresses |journal=[[El Aliso]] |volume=1 |pages=253–321}}</ref>

The foliage is slightly toxic to [[livestock]] and can cause miscarriages in cattle.<ref>{{cite journal |author1=V. Sloss |author2=J. W. Brady |year=1983 |title=Abnormal births in cattle following ingestion of ''Cupressus macrocarpa'' foliage |journal=[[Australian Veterinary Journal]] |volume=60 |issue=7 |page=223 |pmid=6639522 |doi=10.1111/j.1751-0813.1983.tb09593.x}}</ref> Sawn logs are used by many craftspeople, some boat builders and small manufacturers, as a furniture structural material and a decorative wood because of its fine colours, though it must be preserved carefully to prevent the wood from splitting. It is also a fast, hot burning, albeit sparky (therefore not suited to open fires), firewood.

=== In Oceania ===
[[File:Cupressus macrocarpa in Christchurch Botanic Gardens 01.jpg|thumb|Large ''Cupressus macrocarpa'' in [[Christchurch Botanic Gardens]], New Zealand]]
In [[Australia]] and New Zealand, where the tree is simply called macrocarpa, the tree and its [[cultivar]]s are frequently grown as a windbreak tree on farms, usually in rows or shelter belts. The species is also planted in New Zealand as an ornamental tree and, occasionally, as a timber tree. There, finding more favorable growing conditions than in its native range, and in the absence of many native pathogens, it often grows much larger, with trees recorded at over {{convert|40|m|ft|abbr=on}} tall and {{convert|3 |m|ft|abbr=on}} in trunk diameter.<ref name=farjon /><ref name=rushforthc />  One specimen – with a trunk diameter of more than {{convert|4.6|m|ft|abbr=on}} – is considered to be the largest recorded single-stemmed specimen in the world.<ref>{{cite web|title=The New Zealand Tree Register|url=https://register.notabletrees.org.nz/tree/view/963}}</ref>  Macrocarpa timber was used for fence posts on New Zealand farms before [[Electric fence|electric fencing]] became popular.

=== Cultivars ===
[[File:Macrocarpa goldcrest wilma.jpg|thumb|upright|''Cupressus macrocarpa'' 'Goldcrest']]
A number of [[cultivar]]s have been selected for garden use, including Goldcrest, with yellow-green, semi-juvenile foliage (with spreading scale-leaf tips) and Lutea with yellow-green foliage. Goldcrest has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]]<ref>{{cite web|title=''Cupressus macropcarpa'' 'Goldcrest'|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/92589/Cupressus-macrocarpa-Goldcrest/Details|access-date=2020-04-17|publisher=Royal Horticultural Society}}</ref> (confirmed 2017).<ref>{{cite web|date=July 2017|title=AGM Plants - Ornamental|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf|access-date=24 January 2018|publisher=Royal Horticultural Society|page=22}}</ref>

Monterey cypress is one of the parents of the fast-growing cultivated [[Hybrid (biology)|hybrid]] [[Leyland cypress]], ''Cupressus'' × ''Leylandii'', the other parent being [[Callitropsis nootkatensis|Nootka cypress]] (''Callitropsis nootkatensis)''.<ref name="rushforthc" />

''Hesperocyparis macrocarpa'' [[cultivar]]s grown in New Zealand are:<ref>{{cite book |author=Staney J. Palmer |year=1990 |title=Palmer's Manual of Trees, Shrubs and Climbers |publisher=Lancewood Publishing |isbn=0-7316-9415-5}}</ref>
*'Aurea Saligna'—long cascades of weeping, golden-yellow, thread-like foliage on a pyramidal tree
*'Brunniana Aurea'—pillar or conical form with soft rich-golden foliage
*'Gold Rocket'—narrow erect form with golden colouring, slow-growing
*'Golden Pillar'—compact conical tree with dense yellow shoots and foliage
*'Greenstead Magnificent'—dwarf form with blue-green foliage
*'Lambertiana Aurea'—hardy upright form tolerating poor soil and climate conditions

=== Traditional medicine ===
[[Ohlone]] people are reported to have used the foliage in a [[decoction]] as a remedy for [[rheumatism]].<ref name=":02">{{Cite journal |last=Bocek|first=Barbara R.|date=1984|title=Ethnobotany of Costanoan Indians, California, Based on Collections by John P. Harrington|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/4254616|journal=Economic Botany|volume=38|issue=2|pages=248|issn=0013-0001}}</ref>

== Chemistry ==
[[Isocupressic acid]], a [[labdane]] diterpenoid, is an abortifacient component of ''H. macrocarpa''.<ref>{{cite journal |author1=K. Parton |author2=D. Gardner |author3=N. B. Williamson |year=1996 |title=Isocupressic acid, an abortifacient component of ''Cupressus macrocarpa'' |journal=[[New Zealand Veterinary Journal]] |volume=44 |issue=3 |pages= 109–111|doi=10.1080/00480169.1996.35946|url=https://zenodo.org/record/1234401 |pmid=16031906 }}</ref> Monoterpenes (α- and γ-[[terpinene]] and terpinolene) are constituents of the foliage volatile oil.<ref>{{cite journal |author1=Eugene Zavarin |author2=Lorraine Lawrence |author3=Mary C. Thomas |year=1971 |title=Compositional variations of leaf monoterpenes in ''Cupressus macrocarpa'', ''C. pygmaea'', ''C. goveniana'', ''C. abramsiana'' and ''C. sargentii'' |journal=[[Phytochemistry (journal)|Phytochemistry]] |volume=10 |issue=2 |pages=379–393 |doi=10.1016/S0031-9422(00)94053-6|bibcode=1971PChem..10..379Z }}</ref> The oil exact composition is : α-[[pinene]] (20.2%), [[sabinene]] (12.0%), [[p-Cymene]] (7.0%) and [[terpinen-4-ol]] (29.6%).<ref>{{cite journal |author1=Rubén A. Malizia |author2=Daniel A. Cardell |author3=José S. Molli |author4=Silvia González |author5=Pedro E. Guerra |author6=Ricardo J. Grau |year=2000 |title=Volatile constituents of leaf oils from the Cupressaceae family: Part I. ''Cupressus macrocarpa'' Hartw., ''C. arizonica'' Greene and ''C. torulosa'' Don species growing in Argentina |journal=[[Journal of Essential Oil Research]] |volume=12 |issue=1 |pages=59–63 |doi=10.1080/10412905.2000.9712042|s2cid=94802464 }}</ref> Unusual sesquiterpenes can be found in the foliage.<ref>{{cite journal |author=Laurence G. Cool  |year=2005 |title=Sesquiterpenes from ''Cupressus macrocarpa'' foliage |journal=[[Phytochemistry (journal)|Phytochemistry]] |volume=66 |issue=2 |pages=249–260 |doi=10.1016/j.phytochem.2004.11.002|pmid=15652582 |bibcode=2005PChem..66..249C |url=https://zenodo.org/record/894832 }}</ref> Longiborneol (also known as [[juniperol]] or macrocarpol) can also be isolated from Monterey cypresses.<ref>{{cite journal |author1=Steven C. Welch |author2=Roland L. Walters |year=1973 |title=Total syntheses of (+)-longicamphor and (+)-longiborneol |journal=[[Synthetic Communications]] |volume=3 |issue=6 |pages=419–423 |doi=10.1080/00397917308065935}}</ref>
